title: What is the difference between aligned checkpoints (all channels must receive barrier before snapshot, can cause backpressure amplification) and unaligned checkpoints (Flink 1.11+, snapshot includes in-flight data, reduces checkpoint duration under backpressure)?
shortTitle: Aligned vs unaligned checkpoints in Flink

s1_definition.oneliner: Aligned checkpoints wait for all barriers and exclude in-flight data but stall under backpressure, while unaligned checkpoints snapshot immediately including in-flight data to stay fast under backpressure.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Aligned checkpoint** – Operator waits for the barrier on all input channels before snapshotting, buffering fast channels; produces small, clean snapshots but amplifies backpressure when one input is slow.
- **Unaligned checkpoint** – Operator snapshots immediately when the first barrier arrives, including in-flight records from input and output buffers; dramatically shortens checkpoint duration under backpressure.
- **In-flight data** – Records sitting in network buffers that are included in the unaligned snapshot and replayed on recovery.
- **Alignment timeout** – Hybrid setting where Flink starts aligned and switches to unaligned only if alignment takes too long.
- **Trade-off** – Unaligned checkpoints produce larger snapshots and heavier recovery but keep checkpoints reliable when the system is stressed.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants a consistent photo of its processing line. In aligned mode, a clerk fed by two conveyors who sees the colored barrier slip on one freezes that conveyor and waits for the other, which stalls the fast conveyor. In unaligned mode, the clerk takes the photo immediately when the first barrier arrives, including every slip currently in the in-trays and out-trays, so nothing stalls but the photo is bigger.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Aligned vs Unaligned Checkpoint

  Aligned (waits for all barriers):
  Input 1: ─[R1][R2][B42]─────[R3][R4]──▶
                      ▲  STALL  ▲
  Input 2: ─[C1]──────────[C2][B42]──────▶
                                ▲
                          All barriers received
                          NOW snapshot
  ⚠ Input 1 stalled, backpressure upstream

  Unaligned (snapshots immediately):
  Input 1: ─[R1][R2][B42][R3][R4]───────▶
                      ▲
              SNAPSHOT NOW (includes in-flight C1, C2)
  Input 2: ─[C1][C2]────────[B42]───────▶
                              ▲
              B42 overtakes C1, C2
  ✓ No stall, no additional backpressure
  ✓ Larger snapshot (includes in-flight data)

  Hybrid (alignment timeout = 5s):
  Normal:       aligned checkpoint (small)
  Backpressure: switch to unaligned after 5s (fast)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Aligned and unaligned checkpoints are two modes for how multi-input operators snapshot during Flink's barrier-based checkpointing. In aligned mode, when the barrier arrives on one input, the operator stalls that input and waits for barriers on all other inputs before snapshotting. This gives clean, small snapshots but amplifies backpressure because fast channels stall while waiting for slow ones, and under heavy load aligned checkpoints can time out.

Unaligned checkpoints fix this by snapshotting immediately when the first barrier arrives, including the in-flight records in input and output buffers as part of the snapshot. The barrier can overtake buffered records. Because there is no waiting, checkpoints complete quickly even under severe backpressure. The cost is larger snapshots and heavier recovery because in-flight records must be replayed.

The practical sweet spot is the alignment-timeout hybrid: start each checkpoint aligned, and automatically switch to unaligned only if alignment takes too long. This keeps snapshots small during normal operation and pays the larger-snapshot cost only when the system is struggling.

At the National Bank of India an enrichment job joining fast transactions with slow reference data experienced backpressure during market-open spikes. Aligned checkpoints timed out repeatedly. Enabling unaligned checkpoints with a five-second alignment timeout solved the problem: calm periods produced small aligned snapshots, and spikes produced slightly larger unaligned ones that completed reliably.

Remember one sentence: Aligned checkpoints wait for all barriers and amplify backpressure, unaligned checkpoints snapshot immediately with in-flight data to stay fast under load, and the alignment-timeout hybrid is the real-world default.

---

keyPoints: Aligned checkpoints wait for barriers on all input channels before snapshotting, producing small snapshots but amplifying backpressure.
Unaligned checkpoints (Flink 1.11+) snapshot immediately on the first barrier, including in-flight data, eliminating checkpoint stalls.
Unaligned snapshots are larger and recovery is heavier because in-flight records must be replayed.
The alignment-timeout hybrid starts aligned and switches to unaligned only if alignment takes too long, balancing snapshot size and reliability.
Unaligned checkpoints require exactly-once mode and may have version-specific restrictions.
Monitor alignment buffering time to detect when backpressure is causing checkpoint delays.
